Palm of Hand & Wrist — Lecture Companion

Anatomy → biomechanics → vascular/nerve routes → lesion localization. Course learning objectives with clinical reasoning and image identification.

BEFORE YOU START

Learning objectives

  1. Identify and describe the bones, articulations, and associated ligaments of the hand & wrist.
  2. Discuss fascial structures, the carpal tunnel and ulnar canal, and anatomical bases of Dupuytren’s contracture, carpal tunnel syndrome, and ulnar canal syndrome.
  3. Define intrinsic hand muscles, their attachments, actions, and innervation; contrast intrinsic and extrinsic muscles.
  4. Recognize palmar arterial patterns and trace sequential routes of blood flow.
  5. Describe motor and sensory innervation, especially median and ulnar nerve branches and functions.
  6. Identify synovial sheaths and bursae and their clinical importance.
  7. Explain significant hand/wrist injuries: fractures, dislocations, lacerations, ischemia, tenosynovitis, nerve lesions.
  8. Recognize relevant anatomical structures on radiographs, MRI, and CT.

Big picture

This lecture builds a spatial map of the wrist, then uses the map to predict which movements, sensory territories, and blood vessels are affected by injury. Learn the bones and two tunnels first; attach muscle functions and nerve branches; finally interpret clinical signs and imaging.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE 1

Build the skeletal map before learning pathology

The wrist is a radiocarpal condyloid synovial joint. The distal radius articulates with the scaphoid and lunate; the distal radioulnar articular disc (part of the TFCC) articulates with the triquetrum. Crucially, the ulna does not directly articulate with any carpal bone. The TFCC stabilizes the ulnar wrist and helps distribute forces. The distal radioulnar joint is a pivot joint for pronation and supination.

RegionBones / articulationMovement or significance
Proximal row, lateral → medialScaphoid · lunate · triquetrum · pisiformPisiform lies on palmar triquetrum; lunate commonly dislocates
Distal row, lateral → medialTrapezium · trapezoid · capitate · hamateCapitate is largest; hamate hook borders Guyon canal
Thumb CMCTrapezium–first metacarpal; saddle jointFlex/extend, abduct/adduct, circumduct; opposition combines motions
Finger MCPMetacarpal heads–proximal phalanges; condyloidFlex/extend, abduct/adduct, circumduct
PIP / DIPPhalangeal hinge jointsFlex and extend; thumb has only two phalanges

Wrist support includes palmar and dorsal radiocarpal ligaments and radial and ulnar collateral ligaments. The scapholunate ligament is the most commonly torn wrist ligament according to the lecture, particularly after a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH).

MUST KNOW
A scaphoid fracture after FOOSH causes anatomical snuffbox tenderness and threatens the proximal fragment with avascular necrosis; a scapholunate ligament injury may accompany carpal instability and anterior lunate displacement.
CLINICAL CONNECTION
The handout adds Colles fracture: a distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement (“dinner-fork” contour), often after forced dorsiflexion. Scaphoid fracture may be occult on the initial radiograph; the handout notes it can become apparent after 10–14 days.
Why is the ulna excluded from the radiocarpal articular surface? Reveal answer
The triangular fibrocartilage articular disc separates the ulnar head from the proximal carpal row; the disc articulates with the triquetrum.
LEARNING OBJECTIVE 2

Fascia, tunnels, and compressive syndromes

The palmar aponeurosis is a thick sheet of longitudinal fascia extending distally from the flexor retinaculum toward the medial four digits; it is associated proximally with the palmaris longus tendon and sends septa that divide the palm into compartments. Fibrosis and shortening create Dupuytren’s contracture: palmar nodules and cords progressively draw, often, digits 4 and 5 into flexion at MCP/PIP joints.

PassageAnatomical arrangementContents / key distinction
Carpal tunnelCarpal arch floor/walls + flexor retinaculum roofMedian nerve + 9 tendons: FDS ×4, FDP ×4, FPL ×1
Superficial to retinaculumNot within carpal tunnelUlnar nerve and artery, palmar cutaneous median branch, palmaris longus tendon if present
Guyon (ulnar) canalPisiform ↔ hook of hamate and overlying fibrous coveringUlnar nerve + ulnar artery
COMMON CONFUSION
Carpal tunnel compresses the median nerve after the palmar cutaneous branch leaves it; central palm sensation is typically spared. A more proximal median nerve laceration can affect palmar sensation.
CLINICAL CONNECTION
Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median-distribution sensory symptoms and weak/atrophic thenar muscles. The lecture describes surgical release by dividing the flexor retinaculum to reduce pressure. Guyon canal entrapment (“handlebar neuropathy”) instead threatens intrinsic ulnar motor function and medial 1½-digit sensation.
Which contents distinguish the carpal tunnel from Guyon canal? Reveal answer
Carpal tunnel: median nerve plus 9 flexor tendons; Guyon canal: ulnar nerve and artery.
LEARNING OBJECTIVE 3

Intrinsic muscles: movement comes from architecture

Intrinsic muscles originate and insert within the hand and refine grip, opposition, finger spread, and interphalangeal extension. Extrinsic muscles have bellies in the forearm; their long tendons generate more powerful wrist/finger motion (e.g., FDS → middle phalanges/PIP flexion, FDP → distal phalanges/DIP flexion, FPL → distal thumb phalanx). Remember the mirrored thenar/hypothenar functional groups but different nerve supply.

MuscleLecture attachment patternActionInnervation
Abductor pollicis brevis (APB)Flexor retinaculum, scaphoid, trapezium → lateral thumb proximal phalanxThumb abductionRecurrent median
Flexor pollicis brevis (FPB)Flexor retinaculum/scaphoid/trapezium → lateral thumb proximal phalanxThumb flexionSuperficial: recurrent median; deep: deep ulnar
Opponens pollicisFlexor retinaculum/scaphoid/trapezium → first metacarpal shaftThumb opposition / rotationRecurrent median
Abductor digiti minimiPisiform → medial base of fifth proximal phalanxAbduct digit 5Deep ulnar
Flexor digiti minimi brevisFlexor retinaculum/hamate hook → medial fifth proximal phalanxFlex digit 5Deep ulnar
Opponens digiti minimiFlexor retinaculum/hamate hook → fifth metacarpal shaftOppose / rotate digit 5Deep ulnar
Adductor pollicis: oblique + transverse headsOblique: bases MC2/3, capitate, adjacent carpals; transverse: MC3 shaft → medial thumb proximal phalanxThumb adduction; assists oppositionDeep ulnar
Lumbricals 1–4FDP tendons → lateral extensor expansions of digits 2–5Flex MCP + extend PIP/DIP1–2 median; 3–4 deep ulnar

EXAM TRAP
Do not group adductor pollicis with median-innervated thenar muscles. It is deep ulnar. Likewise, FPB deep head is a named ulnar exception.
CLINICAL CONNECTION
For Froment sign, loss of adductor pollicis strength causes compensation by thumb IP flexion when gripping paper. Finger adduction can be tested by holding paper between adjacent fingers; abduction by spreading digits against resistance.
Why does an ulnar nerve injury disrupt finger spreading but usually spare thumb opposition by opponens pollicis? Reveal answer
All interossei are deep-ulnar innervated; opponens pollicis is supplied by recurrent median.
LEARNING OBJECTIVE 4

Trace the arterial circulation, not just its labels

Two connected palmar arterial arches provide overlapping blood supply. The ulnar artery enters via Guyon canal and mainly supplies the superficial arch, deep to the palmar aponeurosis. Its common palmar digital branches split into proper palmar digital arteries. The radial artery travels dorsally through the anatomical snuffbox, passes between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous, and mainly supplies the deep arch. The radial artery also gives princeps pollicis and radialis indicis arteries; its superficial branch can complete the superficial arch. The deep ulnar branch can complete the deep arch.

MUST KNOW
Ulnar → superficial palmar arch → common palmar digital → proper palmar digital. Radial → dorsal snuffbox → first dorsal interosseous interval → deep palmar arch → palmar metacarpal. These arches anastomose.
CLINICAL CONNECTION
Allen test: compress both radial and ulnar arteries, repeatedly open/close hand until blanched, release one artery and observe return of color; repeat for the other. The handout frames this as a test of collateral perfusion before procedures involving either vessel.
Which artery contributes most to each palmar arch? Reveal answer
Ulnar predominates in superficial arch; radial predominates in deep arch.
LEARNING OBJECTIVE 5

Median and ulnar nerve branch maps and lesion levels

Median nerve (lecture: C5–T1): palmar cutaneous branch exits proximal to carpal tunnel (central palm); nerve passes through carpal tunnel; recurrent branch supplies APB, opponens pollicis, and superficial FPB; digital branches supply first two lumbricals and sensation over palmar/distal dorsal surfaces and nail beds of the lateral 3½ digits.

Ulnar nerve (C8–T1): enters through Guyon canal; superficial branch gives digital sensory supply to medial 1½ digits; deep branch supplies hypothenar muscles, interossei, adductor pollicis, medial two lumbricals, and FPB deep head. Dorsal sensory ulnar territory provides an additional lesion-localization clue.

LesionIntrinsic deficitsAdditional proximal deficits / clues
Median at carpal tunnelThenar weakness, reduced opposition; lateral lumbrical weakness, lateral 3½-digit paresthesiaCentral palm spared because palmar cutaneous branch leaves proximally
Median laceration at wrist / palmThenar wasting, loss of thumb opposition and precisionPalmar sensation may be lost with injury proximal to cutaneous branch; isolated recurrent branch laceration can spare digits
Median at elbowSame distal deficitsFDS, lateral FDP, FPL and pronators impaired → difficult fist / hand of benediction on attempted fist
Ulnar at Guyon canalInterossei, medial lumbricals, adductor pollicis, hypothenar weakUlnar claw of digits 4–5; FDP/FCU forearm motor preserved
Ulnar at elbowSame intrinsic deficitsAdds FCU and medial FDP weakness, impaired DIP flexion digits 4–5; may deviate radially with wrist flexion
COMMON CONFUSION
Benediction = median injury apparent when trying to make a fist. Ulnar claw = intrinsic ulnar injury apparent with hand open / attempted finger extension. Clinical presentation depends on lesion level.
A patient loses finger abduction and has weakness in paper pinch. Which nerve branch is implicated? Reveal answer
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (interossei + adductor pollicis).
LEARNING OBJECTIVE 6

Flexor sheaths and clinical spread of infection

Fibrous digital sheaths secure long flexor tendons near the phalanges, acting as pulleys; internal synovial sheaths provide a low-friction gliding surface. The lecturer identifies flexor tenosynovitis as swelling, pain, and inflammation of tendon plus sheath. The handout makes the clinically important continuity distinction: digits 2–4 generally have separate sheaths, whereas the fifth digital synovial sheath is continuous with the common flexor sheath, so infection can track proximally through the palm/carpal tunnel toward anterior forearm.

CLINICAL CONNECTION
Painful swollen digits after penetrating injury require concern for flexor sheath infection; the anatomic sheath network predicts the route of spread.
Which finger has a sheath continuous with the common flexor sheath in the handout? Reveal answer
Digit 5; therefore infection may spread proximally into the palm and anterior forearm.
LEARNING OBJECTIVE 7

Predict deficits from the injury site

Think site → endangered structure → lost function → examination sign. The same fall can injure bone (scaphoid, distal radius), ligament (scapholunate), or displace a carpal bone (lunate); symptoms follow the neighboring neurovascular structures. Palm lacerations may directly injure the superficial recurrent median branch; hamate hook trauma puts the ulnar bundle near Guyon canal at risk.

ProblemAnatomic mechanismSignature finding
Scaphoid fractureFOOSH → scaphoid disruption / jeopardized proximal blood supplySnuffbox pain, risk proximal AVN
Lunate dislocationAnterior displacement toward carpal tunnelMedian nerve symptoms, possible ischemic injury
Scapholunate sprainFOOSH tears key intercarpal ligamentWrist pain/instability; may be linked with lunate displacement in lecture
Distal radius Colles fractureDorsally displaced distal radial fragmentDinner-fork deformity
Hook of hamate fractureNear ulnar canal contents; hypothenar tractionUlnar nerve/artery risk, reduced grip
Median recurrent branch cutSuperficial lateral palm injuryThumb opposition/abduction weakness
Flexor tenosynovitisInflammation in tendon sheathPainful swollen finger; digit 5 may spread proximally
Vascular compromiseInsufficient radial/ulnar collateralsReduced palm reperfusion on Allen test
FIRST AID CONNECTION
Scaphoid fracture: clinical suspicion persists with snuffbox tenderness even when the initial plain film is unrevealing. The handout explicitly notes delayed X-ray visibility; apply that principle when interpreting clinical vignettes.
LECTURE → STEP 1 BRIDGE
FOOSH → scaphoid injury → proximal fragment blood supply interruption → avascular necrosis. Or hamate hook injury → ulnar neuropathy → interosseous/adductor pollicis weakness → impaired finger spread / Froment sign.
After a hook of hamate fracture, which motor functions are most at risk? Reveal answer
Deep-branch ulnar functions: interosseous-mediated abduction/adduction, adductor pollicis, hypothenar function, and medial lumbricals.
LEARNING OBJECTIVE 8

Recognize structures in cross-section and clinical imaging

Begin every image by establishing modality, plane, and laterality. On an AP wrist radiograph, identify distal radius/ulna, both carpal rows, capitate in line with third metacarpal, and the scapholunate interval; a proximal carpal injury changes alignment. On an axial wrist MRI or CT, locate the carpal arch, palmar flexor retinaculum, flexor tendons, median nerve, and superficial ulnar neurovascular canal.

PRACTICAL IMAGE
On radiographs trace scaphoid → lunate → triquetrum and trapezium → trapezoid → capitate → hamate. On axial images, identify the flexor retinaculum as the roof, with median nerve deep to it and ulnar nerve/artery superficial and medial. The slides show X-ray and MRI examples; they do not provide a separate labeled CT case.
On an axial wrist MRI, is the ulnar nerve expected inside the carpal tunnel? Reveal answer
No. It courses through Guyon canal, superficial to the flexor retinaculum.
SYNTHESIS

Master these before moving on

  1. Carpal rows + radiocarpal surfaces: know where radius/TFCC articulate; explains FOOSH injury localization and instability.
  2. Carpal tunnel vs Guyon canal: different contents and different sensory/motor consequences.
  3. Median vs deep ulnar intrinsic supply: thumb opposition versus thumb adduction; PAD/DAB and lumbrical split.
  4. Proximal versus distal nerve injury: forearm flexors change the clinical sign and hand posture.
  5. Superficial versus deep arches: artery dominance plus connected collateral supply explains Allen testing.

Most useful First Aid connections

These are narrow, lecture-adjacent board links, not additional lecture objectives:

  1. Scaphoid FOOSH + snuffbox pain → proximal fragment avascular necrosis risk.
  2. Median nerve entrapment in carpal tunnel → thenar deficits, central palm sensation spared.
  3. Ulnar neuropathy in Guyon canal → interosseous weakness, paper-grip deficit/Froment sign.
  4. Median elbow lesion versus wrist lesion → hand of benediction on attempted fist only with proximal flexor loss.
